label: prop:markov-trace-recursive-reducer
title: Existence of a recursive symbolic Markov-trace reducer for $H_n(q)$ with disjoint-product property
html:
Let \beta \in B_n be any braid word. There is a terminating structural recursion on words that returns a closed-form symbolic expression for \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) \in \mathbb{Q}(q) using only:

  • the Hecke quadratic \sigma_i^2 = h \sigma_i + 1 (with h = q - q^{-1});
  • the Markov axiom \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \sigma_n) = z \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha) for \alpha \in H_n \subset H_{n+1}, for the Markov parameter z;
  • cyclicity \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha\beta) = \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta\alpha);
  • and the braid relations.

The trace it computes has the disjoint-product property. Number the generators from 1. Let \alpha be a word in \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_{k+1} and \beta a word in \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_m, and write \beta^{\uparrow} for \beta with every generator index raised by k+1, so that \beta^{\uparrow} uses \sigma_{k+2}, \ldots, \sigma_{k+m+1}. Then

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \beta^{\uparrow}) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta).

The two clusters share the strand k+2.

The split form also holds: \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \otimes \beta) = \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) for \alpha \in H_k(q) on strands \{1, \ldots, k\} and \beta \in H_{n-k-1}(q) on strands \{k+2, \ldots, n\}, separated by the unused generator \sigma_{k+1}.

Correctness follows from uniqueness on positive words: any two linear functionals satisfying these axioms with the same z and h agree on every positive braid word, and since \sigma_i^{-1} = \sigma_i - h, positive words determine the trace on all of B_n. Conversely, defining the evaluator by structural recursion on positive words yields a terminating procedure that is normalised on the empty word, stable under strand addition, invariant under strand shift \sigma_a \mapsto \sigma_{a+j}, and compatible with the Hecke quadratic relation, far commutation, the braid relation, Markov stabilisation, and—by Ocneanu's induction on the strand index—cyclicity. This establishes existence of the Markov trace for arbitrary z and h, and uniqueness identifies every trace satisfying the axioms with the recursive evaluator. Shift invariance \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta^{\uparrow}) = \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) is the shared-strand law with \alpha empty, from which the split disjoint-product formula follows.

The algorithm and its correctness are parametric in z: no step below evaluates the Markov parameter, so the statement holds for whatever value the Markov axiom is given. Production evaluates it at z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1). This is worth stating explicitly because the statement previously fixed z to 1/(q^{1/2}+q^{-1/2}) inside a claim that never used it, which made a convention choice look like a hypothesis of the theorem.

Proof — the algorithm

Input: braid word \beta = \sigma_{i_1}^{\varepsilon_1} \cdots \sigma_{i_m}^{\varepsilon_m} with \varepsilon_j \in \{\pm 1\} and 1 \leq i_j \leq n - 1.

Step 1 (Hecke expansion). Expand \beta into the standard Iwahori-Hecke basis T_w for w \in S_n:

  \beta \;=\; \sum_{w \in S_n} c_w(q) T_w.

Step 2 (recursive basis-element trace). For each w \in S_n appearing with non-zero coefficient, compute \mathrm{tr}_M(T_w) recursively:

def tr_M(perm, n):
    if perm == identity:
        return 1
    word = canonical_reduced_word(perm)          # 0-indexed gens
    max_gen = max(word)                          # ∈ {0, …, n-2}
    if max_gen < n - 2:
        # w ∈ H_{max_gen+2} ⊂ H_n; truncate.
        return tr_M(perm[:max_gen+2], max_gen+2)
    # max_gen == n-2: peel σ_{n-2} via Markov axiom + cyclicity.
    k = rightmost position of max_gen in word
    rotated = word[k+1:] + word[:k]              # length ℓ(w) - 1
    # Reduce `rotated` back into the H_n basis (may involve
    # Hecke quadratic firings if σ_{n-2} re-appears).
    E = expand_in_hecke_basis(rotated, n)
    return z * Σ_{w' ∈ E} c_{w'} · tr_M(T_{w'}, n)

Step 3 (combine). Output \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) = \sum_w c_w \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(T_w).

Correctness

Termination. Each invocation of the recursive \mathrm{tr}_M call either: (i) truncates the ambient algebra (n \to \text{max\_gen} + 2 where \text{max\_gen} + 2 < n), strictly decreasing the integer n; or (ii) peels one \sigma_{n-2} from the word and recurses on basis elements w' with \ell(w') \leq \ell(\text{rotated}) = \ell(w) - 1, strictly decreasing the Coxeter length.

The lex order on (n, \ell(w)) has no infinite descending chain, so termination is guaranteed. Each basis expansion involves at most n! basis elements; no bound on the total number of evaluations is proved here. \square

Correctness. Each step is an exact equality in \mathbb{Q}(q):

  • Step 1 is exact (Hecke-quadratic expansion).
  • The truncation case (max_gen < n - 2) uses the embedding H_{n-1} \hookrightarrow H_n. This preserves \mathrm{tr}_M (the Markov axiom yields the same value regardless of ambient algebra, by stability of z).
  • The peeling case uses cyclicity to put \sigma_{n-2} at the rightmost position. The Markov axiom then contributes a z factor. The remainder \alpha \beta (with \alpha, \beta on either side of the rotated cut) need not lie in H_{n-1} if \alpha contained another \sigma_{n-2}. In that case, the basis-expansion subroutine handles the Hecke-quadratic firings exactly.

By induction on (n, \ell), the output equals \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) in \mathbb{Q}(q). \square

Disjoint-product property

Write \beta^{\uparrow} for \beta with every generator index raised by k+1, so that \alpha uses \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_{k+1} and \beta^{\uparrow} uses \sigma_{k+2}, \ldots. Then

  \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \beta^{\uparrow}) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha) \cdot \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta).

The proof is by induction on the number m of generators of \beta, with Ocneanu's reduction inside each level. Fix \alpha and let F(\beta) be the difference of the two sides. Both sides satisfy the Hecke quadratic, braid and far-commutation relations in any context, so F does too.

  • If \beta avoids its top generator \sigma_{m}, stability lowers m on both sides, and the induction hypothesis gives F(\beta) = 0.
  • If \beta = a\,\sigma_{m}\,b uses it once, cyclicity moves b^{\uparrow} to the front, the Markov axiom strips the top letter with a factor z, and cyclicity restores \alpha (ab)^{\uparrow}. The same steps on the right side give z\,\mathrm{tr}_M(ab), and the induction hypothesis closes the case.
  • If \beta uses \sigma_m twice or more, take two consecutive occurrences \sigma_m x \sigma_m. If x avoids \sigma_{m-1}, far commutation brings the two letters together and the quadratic relation shortens the word. If x uses \sigma_{m-1} once, one braid move removes a \sigma_m. Otherwise x is first reduced one level down by the same argument.

Every function on words that satisfies the three relations and vanishes on words using the top generator at most once therefore vanishes, so F = 0. Both clusters share the strand k+2, so the closures form a connected sum.

For the split form, let \alpha \in H_k use \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_{k-1} and let \beta_0 be \beta written on \sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_{n-k-2}. Apply the shared-strand law with k-1 in place of k to \alpha and to \beta', the word \beta_0 with every index raised by 1; then \beta'^{\uparrow} is \beta on strands \{k+2, \ldots, n\}, and the law gives \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha \otimes \beta) = \mathrm{tr}_M(\alpha)\,\mathrm{tr}_M(\beta'). Shift invariance gives \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta') = \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta_0); it is the shared-strand law applied with \alpha the empty word, since \mathrm{tr}_M(1) = 1.

Which axioms the disjoint product actually needs

Scope of the right-induction step. Right-induction yields z^{\ell(\beta)} directly only when every generator in \beta occurs with multiplicity one; for general words containing repeated generators (such as \sigma_1^2, where \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2) = hz + 1 \neq z^2), the disjoint-product reduction alternates right-peeling with the quadratic Hecke relation \sigma_i^2 = h\sigma_i + 1.

The argument above is stated in terms of the Markov axiom and cyclicity, but it uses two further properties silently, and both are named in the correctness section: normalisation \mathrm{tr}_M(1) = 1, and stability under the trivial embedding — "the Markov axiom yields the same value regardless of ambient algebra". Neither follows from stripping and cyclicity.

Stripping and cyclicity alone admit a counter-model. Put \mathrm{tr}_M on H_n equal to 2^n for every word, with z = 2. Stripping holds, since 2^{n+1} = 2 \cdot 2^n; cyclicity holds because both sides ignore the word. The product law fails at k = 0, n = 2, \alpha = \beta = 1, where the left side is 4 and the right is 2^0 \cdot 2^1 = 2. So a trace that grows with the ambient index alone is not excluded by stripping and rearrangement.

Normalisation and stability are therefore part of the axiom set, but they are not enough either: if stripping, stability and cyclicity are quantified over every word, they force \mathrm{tr}_M(\beta) = z^{\ell(\beta)}, which contradicts \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2) = hz + 1. The axiom set therefore restricts stripping, stability and cyclicity to words of H_n and adds the Hecke quadratic, braid and far-commutation relations. From these axioms it proves \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_n^2) = hz + 1 and the product law when \beta is an ascending run \sigma_{k+1}\cdots\sigma_{k+m}, and the general product law by the reduction in the previous section.

Empirical verification

atom braid word H_n \mathrm{tr}_M(q_0)
proton \sigma_1^7 \sigma_2^4 H_3 1.884319\ldots
neutron \sigma_1^6 \sigma_2^4 \sigma_1^{-1} H_3 1.464034\ldots
deuteron disjoint \sigma_1^7\sigma_2^4 \oplus \sigma_4^6\sigma_5^4\sigma_4^{-1} H_6 \mathrm{tr}_M(p)\cdot\mathrm{tr}_M(n)

The two numeric entries are evaluated at z = q^{3}/(q^{2}+1). They are not nucleon mass inputs: these braid words are not the canonical nucleon words, so the values must not be used for mass predictions.

The producer additionally checks the closed forms the Markov axioms force — \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_i) = z, \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1\sigma_2) = z^2, \mathrm{tr}_M(\sigma_1^2) = hz + 1, and z^3, z^4 on the H_4 and H_5 chains — together with the disjoint-product identity above, evaluated as \mathrm{tr}_M(H_6;\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_4\sigma_5) against \mathrm{tr}_M(H_3;\sigma_1\sigma_2)^2. All nine agree to the working precision. These are the substantive checks: each is a prediction of the axioms that the reducer reaches by an independent route (Hecke-basis expansion, then recursive descent), whereas the two table entries above have no independent reference to be checked against.

References

  • [Jones 1987] Hecke algebra representations of braid groups and link polynomials, Annals of Math. 126, 335-388.
  • [Kassel 1995] Quantum Groups, Springer GTM 155, Ch. III §3.
  • [Wenzl 1988] Hecke algebras of type A_n and subfactors, Inventiones Math. 92, 349-383.
